title: Defend It
bigQuestion: What does it take to stand behind an argument out loud, in front of people who are free to push back?

story.title: The First Question Is the Hard One
story.kicker: Twelve minutes to present a semester of work, and then the floor opens to a room that has been waiting to ask.
paragraphs: Dani had twelve minutes. She knew, because she had rehearsed the talk nine times with a timer, and the last three runs had come in at eleven and a half. Her slides were ready: seven of them, mostly images, one map, one quotation, no paragraphs. Her notes were a single index card. She walked to the front of the classroom, plugged in, and looked at twenty-six people who had all read the assignment and knew what a weak talk sounded like. Then she started with the street sign.

The talk went the way the rehearsals had gone, which is the whole point of rehearsing. She told the story of the name, showed the map of where families had moved from, read the one quotation from the parish history and let it sit for a beat, and closed on her thesis: the name survived because each community found its own reasons to keep it. Eleven minutes and forty seconds. She said thank you. Hands went up.

The first hand belonged to Jordan, who had written a paper on the same neighborhood from a different angle. Jordan said, politely, that Dani's argument seemed to leave out money. Landlords and developers had reasons to keep a name that sounded historic, and those reasons were not about community at all. Wasn't the real story about who profited from the name, not who loved it? It was a good question. It was, in fact, the objection Dani had spent a page on in her paper and had cut from the talk for time.

She felt the pull that every presenter feels: to agree quickly and make the question go away. She did not. She said that Jordan was right that developers had used the name, that her sixth source documented exactly that in the 1990s, and that she had decided it did not explain the earlier decades, when nobody was profiting and the name still held. Then she said what she did not know: whether the money story became the main story after 2000. Jordan nodded. The next hand went up.

This chapter is about that room: how to build a talk that fits its time, how to put evidence on a screen without reading it aloud, how to expect the hard question and answer it without folding or bluffing, how to argue with classmates in a way that improves everyone's thinking, how to listen and give feedback that is actually useful, and what to carry out of this course into whatever you do next.
story.think: Dani conceded part of Jordan's point and held the rest. Why is that stronger than either agreeing completely or refusing to give any ground?

lessons.title: Structure for the Ear
lessons.mainIdea: A listener cannot reread, so a talk needs fewer points, a clearer map, and more repetition than a paper.
reading: A reader who loses the thread of your paper can flip back a page. A listener who loses the thread of your talk is gone, and there is no page to flip. That single difference changes everything about how a talk is built. A twelve-page paper might make five claims with twenty pieces of evidence. A twelve-minute talk on the same paper should make one claim with three pieces of evidence, chosen because they are the strongest and the easiest to picture. Turning a paper into a talk is not compression. It is selection.

Give the ear a map. Say early what you will argue and how many parts the argument has: I will show three things. First, that the name was contested from the start. Second, that both communities found reasons to keep it. Third, that those reasons were different. Then, as you reach each part, say so: that was the first point, and here is the second. This is *signposting* for the ear, and it is more necessary than it is on the page. Listeners who know where they are can relax and follow; listeners who do not spend their attention trying to guess.

Open with something specific: a scene, an object, a question, a number. Dani began with a street sign. A talk that opens with Today I am going to talk about my research paper has already lost the room. Close the way you opened, by returning to the specific thing and showing what it means now that the argument is made. The middle carries the evidence, one piece at a time, each introduced, shown and explained, exactly as a quotation is framed in a paper. Between pieces, pause. Silence that feels long to you feels like thinking time to the audience.

Repeat more than feels natural. In a paper, saying the thesis three times reads as padding. In a talk, saying it at the start, at the turn into each point and at the end is the minimum, because a listener who missed it once has no other way to get it. Use the same words each time so it lands as the same idea. The talk's *through-line*, the one sentence a listener should be able to repeat afterward, must be short enough to remember and said often enough to stick.

words.d: telling listeners where the talk is and where it is going: first, second, here is the last point
the one sentence a listener should be able to repeat after the talk is over
choosing the few strongest points and pieces of evidence from a longer work for a talk

rows: Pieces of evidence in the paper
Pieces of evidence in the talk
Times the thesis is stated in the paper
Times the thesis is stated in the talk
look.cite: Dani's paper and talk, counted for this lesson
look.prompt: The talk has fewer claims and less evidence but states the thesis more often. Explain each of those choices in terms of what a listener can and cannot do.

check.q: Why does a talk need more repetition than a paper?
choices: Because audiences are less intelligent than readers
Because a listener who misses a point cannot go back to it
Because talks are graded on length
check.why: There is no page to flip; repetition is the listener's only second chance.

check.q: The lesson says turning a paper into a talk is not compression but selection. What does that mean?
choices: Choose the few strongest points and drop the rest
check.why: A talk keeps one claim and the best evidence rather than squeezing in everything.

check.q: Which opening does the lesson prefer?
choices: Today I am going to talk about my research paper.
A specific scene, object, question or number
check.why: A concrete opening earns attention; an announcement loses it.

lessons.title: Evidence on the Screen
lessons.mainIdea: Slides exist to show what words cannot, so each slide should carry one image, one number or one short quotation, never a paragraph to be read aloud.
reading: Picture two slides. The first holds six bullet points, each a full sentence, in small type; the speaker turns toward it and reads. The second holds a photograph of a church sign in two languages, and the speaker, facing the audience, says what it shows. The first slide competes with the speaker: the audience reads faster than anyone can talk, finishes, and waits, bored. The second slide helps the speaker: it shows a thing that words alone would take a paragraph to describe. That is the test for every slide. Does it show something speech cannot?

A good slide carries one thing. One map, with the one route you are about to describe marked on it. One number, large, with a short label: 2 languages, 20 years. One quotation of a sentence or two, in type big enough to read from the back row, with the source under it. One chart with one line. If you want the audience to look at two things, make two slides. The *one-idea rule* keeps the audience's eyes and the speaker's voice on the same point at the same moment.

Evidence on a screen must be cited just as it is on a page. Put the source in small type on the slide: the author, the title, the year, and for a quotation the page. A photograph needs a credit; a chart needs to say where the numbers came from. Audiences trust speakers who cite, and challengers, as Dani learned, will ask exactly where a claim came from. A slide that already answers is a defense you built in advance. Put a *reference slide* at the end with every source, so you can show it if asked.

When you show a quotation, do not read it aloud. Let the audience read it while you stay silent for a few seconds, then say what it shows. Reading a slide aloud tells the audience that you do not trust them to read, and it wastes the talk's scarcest resource, your voice. Face the room, not the screen; if you need to see the slide, use the laptop. A speaker's notes belong on a card or the presenter view, never on the slide. Finally, plan for the screen to fail. A talk that cannot survive a dead projector was never a talk; it was a slideshow with a narrator.

words.d: each slide carries a single image, number, quotation or chart, so eyes and voice stay on the same point
a final slide listing every source used in the talk, ready to show if asked
the line naming where a photograph, chart or quotation came from

look.title: Seven Slides
look.text: Dani's deck: (1) a photo of the Eighteenth Street sign; (2) a map with one arrow from the Near West Side to Pilsen; (3) the number 2, labeled languages, one parish; (4) a photo of a mural; (5) a single quoted sentence from the parish history with its citation; (6) her thesis in twelve words; (7) references.
look.prompt: Which slides show something words could not? Is there any slide you would cut, and what would you put in its place?

check.q: What is the test the lesson gives for whether a slide belongs in a talk?
choices: Does it show something speech cannot?
Does it contain at least five bullet points?
Does it match the paper's headings?
check.why: Slides earn their place by showing, not by repeating what the speaker says.

check.q: Why does reading a bullet-point slide aloud fail?
choices: Because bullets are not allowed in academic talks
Because the audience reads faster than the speaker talks, finishes, and waits
Because slides cannot be read from the back
check.why: The slide competes with the speaker instead of helping.

check.q: What should a speaker do while a quotation is on screen?
choices: Advance quickly to the next slide
Stay silent a few seconds while the audience reads, then explain what it shows
check.why: Let the audience read, then add the interpretation only the speaker can give.

lessons.title: Timing and Rehearsal
lessons.mainIdea: A talk that fits its time is built by rehearsing out loud with a clock, cutting until there is slack, and planning what to drop if time runs short.
reading: Dani's first rehearsal ran nineteen minutes for a twelve-minute slot. That is typical. Nearly every first draft of a talk runs long, because everything in the paper seems necessary and speaking takes longer than reading. The only way to know is to say it out loud, standing up, with a timer running, from the first word to the last. Reading the notes silently and estimating does not work; people speak at roughly 120 to 150 words a minute, slower when nervous and pausing for slides, and silent reading is far faster than that.

Cut until the rehearsal comes in under time with slack, about a minute in twelve. Cut whole points before you trim sentences; a talk with three complete points beats a talk with five rushed ones. Cut anything the audience can get from the paper if they want it. Then rehearse again. Dani's runs went nineteen, sixteen, fourteen, thirteen, twelve and a half, then three runs near eleven and a half. By the last runs she was no longer reading her card; she was talking, and the card was a safety net. That is what *rehearsal* is for: not memorizing words, but knowing the path so well that you can look at the room while you walk it.

Plan for time to go wrong anyway. Mark one point in your notes as the *cut point*: if you reach it with less than a third of your time left, skip to the conclusion. A talk that runs over its time tells the audience that the speaker's time matters more than theirs, and it usually means the ending, the most important minute, gets rushed or lost. Ending a minute early with a clear conclusion looks like control. Ending two minutes late with an apology looks like the opposite, even when the content was good.

The last rehearsal should be in front of a person, with the real slides, using the real clicker or keyboard, in the real room if you can get into it. Ask the listener to raise a hand every time they lose the thread or cannot see something on a slide. Record yourself once, and watch it, even though you will hate it. You will see the filler words, the hands in the pockets, the turn toward the screen. Fix two things, not ten. Then stop rehearsing the night before; a talk that has been run nine times does not improve with a tenth at midnight.

words.d: practicing a talk out loud, standing, with a timer, until the path is known well enough to look at the room
a marked spot in the notes where a speaker who is running out of time skips ahead to the conclusion
the minute or so of unused time a well-timed talk keeps in reserve

look.title: Nine Rehearsals
look.cite: Dani's rehearsal log, written for this lesson
look.prompt: The biggest drop came between runs 1 and 2. What kind of cut probably produced it, and why did the last runs stop getting shorter?

check.q: Why does silently reading your notes not tell you how long a talk will run?
choices: Because notes are always too short
Because silent reading is much faster than speaking, which runs around 120 to 150 words a minute
Because timers do not work on notes
Because rehearsal must be done in the real room
check.why: Speech, pauses and slides take far longer than silent reading.

check.q: When cutting a long talk, what does the lesson say to cut first?
check.why: Three complete points beat five rushed ones.

check.q: What is the cut point for?
choices: Marking where to insert a joke
Marking where the audience may ask questions
Marking where to skip to the conclusion if time is running out
check.why: It protects the ending, the talk's most important minute, when time goes wrong.

lessons.title: Anticipating the Questions
lessons.mainIdea: The hard questions can be predicted from your own paper's weak points, and the best answers are prepared before anyone raises a hand.
reading: Jordan's question about money did not surprise Dani, because she had written it down two days earlier. Before the talk she had made a list titled What will they ask? It had nine questions on it. Three came from the objection section of her own paper. Two came from evidence she had cut for time. Two came from what a skeptic would say about her sources: an oral history is one person's memory; a newspaper feature is not a study. One was the question she most feared, and one was the question she hoped someone would ask. Jordan's was number two.

Predicting questions is not a trick; it is the same skill as addressing the objection in a paper. Reread your paper as your harshest fair reader. Where is the evidence thinnest? Which source would an expert doubt? What did you claim that goes a step past what the evidence shows? What obvious alternative explanation did you set aside, and why? Where did you cut something for time that a listener will notice is missing? Each answer is a likely question. Write it down as the listener would say it, and write a three-sentence answer beneath it. This is your *question bank*.

Some questions you can answer in advance by building the answer into the talk. If you know your oral history source is vulnerable, say so yourself, briefly: this is one woman's memory, and I use it for what she felt, not for dates. A speaker who names the weakness first has taken it away from the questioner. Others are better left for the questions, because answering them well in front of the room shows the depth of your work; keep a *backup slide* for those, ready to show after the reference slide.

Prepare for the question you cannot answer, too, because it will come. The honest response has three parts: say that you do not know, say what you would need to find out, and, if you can, say how it would or would not affect your thesis. That is not a failure. It is what expertise sounds like. The presenter who bluffs an answer and is caught loses everything said before; the presenter who says I did not look at that, and here is what it would take, keeps the room's trust and usually gets a nod.

words.d: a written list of the questions an audience is likely to ask, each with a prepared short answer
a slide kept after the references, ready to show if a particular question is asked
a different account of the same evidence that a challenger might prefer

look.title: Reading Your Own Paper as a Skeptic
look.text: A paper argues that a school's new later start time improved attendance, using attendance figures from one semester before and one after. The writer lists the questions a skeptic would ask before anyone asks them.
look.prompt: Write three questions a fair skeptic would ask about that evidence, and a three-sentence answer to one of them.

check.q: Where did most of Dani's predicted questions come from?
choices: Her own paper's objection section, cut evidence and vulnerable sources
check.why: The paper's weak points, read as a skeptic, predict the questions.

check.q: Why might a speaker name a source's weakness during the talk itself?
choices: To take the point away from a questioner and show honesty
Because weak sources must be removed
check.why: Naming the limit first shows control and removes the easy challenge.

check.q: What does the lesson say to do with a question you cannot answer?
choices: Say you do not know, say what you would need to find out, and say how it would affect the thesis
Ask the questioner to email you
check.why: An honest, specific I do not know keeps the room's trust; a bluff loses it.

lessons.title: Answering Without Folding
lessons.mainIdea: Answer a challenge by restating it fairly, conceding what is true, holding what the evidence supports, and marking clearly where each part ends.
reading: Two answers to Jordan's question. First: Yes, you are right, I probably should have included that. Second: You are right that developers used the name, and my sixth source shows it happening in the 1990s. But that does not explain the earlier decades, when no one was profiting and the name still held. So I think money is part of the later story, not the whole story. The first answer folds: it gives up a thesis that a semester of evidence supports because a question sounded confident. The second concedes exactly what is true and keeps exactly what the evidence keeps. That is the shape of a good answer.

Start by restating the question in your own words, briefly. This does three things: it shows the room you listened, it gives you five seconds to think, and it lets the questioner correct you if you misheard. Then *concede* what deserves conceding, specifically. A vague you make a good point sounds like a dodge; a specific you are right that the 1990s look different sounds like a scholar. Then say what you hold and why, pointing to evidence: my sixth source, the dates in the map, the parish records. End by saying where the line is: part, not whole; later, not earlier; likely, not certain.

Two failures sit on either side of that shape. Folding is one: agreeing with everything, apologizing, abandoning the claim. It feels polite and it is actually a kind of disrespect, because it tells the questioner that the argument was never serious. *Stonewalling* is the other: refusing to concede anything, repeating the thesis louder, treating the question as an attack. It feels strong and reads as fragile. The room can tell the difference between a speaker defending evidence and a speaker defending pride.

Tone carries as much as content. Thank the questioner once, sincerely, not after every question. Keep your voice at talk volume, not argument volume. Look at the questioner while restating, then at the whole room while answering, because the answer is for everyone. If the question is hostile, answer the content and ignore the tone; the room will notice who stayed calm. And if a question changes your mind, say so on the spot. I had not thought of it that way, and I think that weakens my third point, is a sentence that costs nothing and earns a great deal.

words.d: to admit that a specific part of a challenge is correct
refusing to concede anything, repeating a claim instead of engaging the question
abandoning a supported claim because a question sounded confident
putting a questioner's point into your own words before answering it

look.title: An Answer in Four Moves
look.text: If I understand you, you are asking whether the interview can carry the weight I put on it. Partly it cannot: one memory is not a record of dates. What it can carry is how the name felt to someone who lived under it for sixty years, and I use it only for that. The dates come from the parish records and the map.
look.cite: model answer written for this lesson
look.prompt: Label the four moves: restate, concede, hold, mark the line. Which sentence would be lost if the speaker folded, and which if the speaker stonewalled?

check.q: What is wrong with the answer 'Yes, you are right, I probably should have included that'?
choices: It is rude to the questioner.
It folds, giving up a supported thesis because the question sounded confident.
check.why: Conceding everything abandons evidence that still stands.

check.q: Why restate a question before answering it?
choices: To show you listened, to gain thinking time, and to let the questioner correct a misunderstanding
To use up the question period
Because restating counts as an answer
To make the question sound weaker
check.why: Restating serves the room, the speaker and the questioner at once.

check.q: A speaker repeats the thesis louder and concedes nothing. The lesson calls this what?
check.why: Refusing to engage the question reads as fragile, not strong.

lessons.title: Discussion at a High Level
lessons.mainIdea: A high-level discussion builds on what others said, names disagreements precisely, and moves the group toward a better answer than anyone brought in.
reading: After the talks, the class sat in a circle to discuss a question that cut across all of them: when a neighborhood changes, who gets to say what its history is? Two kinds of discussion could follow. In the first, each student says a prepared opinion, the next student says an unrelated one, and the teacher moves it along. In the second, the third speaker begins with Jordan said profit and Dani said community, and I think the parish records show a third thing, and by the end of the hour the group holds a view none of them walked in with. The second is what *collaborative discussion* means.

The core move is *building*: connecting what you say to what was just said. Agree and extend: Dani's point about the church applies to the schools too, because. Disagree and explain: I read that source differently, since. Ask for more: Jordan, when you say profit, do you mean rents or the name on new buildings? Each of these names a previous speaker and shows what you took from them. A comment that could have been made before the discussion started, with no reference to anything anyone said, is not discussion; it is a speech.

Disagreement is the point, not the problem. A group that agrees quickly has usually just stopped thinking. But disagree with precision. Say which claim you doubt, which evidence makes you doubt it, and what would change your mind. I disagree with everything Jordan said is useless; I think the profit motive is real but starts too late to explain the 1970s is something the group can test. Keep the disagreement on the claim, never on the person. In a good discussion nobody wins, because the goal is not victory but a better answer.

Someone has to tend the discussion, and it should not always be the teacher. Notice who has not spoken and make room: Marcus, you wrote about the murals; does this match what you found? Notice when the group has drifted and bring it back to the question. Notice when two people are saying the same thing in different words and say so. Near the end, someone should try to state what the group now thinks, including where it still splits. The ability to do that, to summarize a live argument fairly, is rare and valued everywhere, from seminar rooms to job sites.

words.d: a conversation in which speakers build on one another to reach a better answer than any one brought in
connecting your comment to what a previous speaker said: extending, questioning or disagreeing with it by name
in disagreement, naming the exact claim, the evidence against it and what would change your mind

look.title: Four Comments in a Circle
look.text: (a) I think history belongs to whoever lives there now. (b) Building on Dani, if the parish kept both languages, then the two communities were sharing the history, not passing it. (c) Jordan, when you say developers, which decade are you talking about? (d) Murals are important too.
look.prompt: Which comments build on the discussion and which could have been said before it started? Rewrite (d) so it builds.

check.q: What makes a comment count as building?
choices: It is longer than a sentence.
It connects by name to what a previous speaker said and extends, questions or disagrees with it.
It introduces a completely new topic.
check.why: Building means the comment could not have been made before the discussion began.

check.q: According to the lesson, what does quick agreement in a group usually mean?
check.why: Disagreement is where a group's thinking happens; fast consensus often means it skipped that step.

check.q: Which is the most precise disagreement?
choices: I disagree with everything Jordan said.
I do not think that is right.
The profit motive is real but starts too late to explain the 1970s.
check.why: It names the claim, the problem with it, and gives the group something to test.

lessons.title: Listening to Evaluate
lessons.mainIdea: Evaluative listening tracks a speaker's claim, evidence and reasoning as they go by, and judges the argument rather than the delivery.
reading: Marcus watched Dani's talk with a page split into three columns: claim, evidence, reasoning. Under claim he wrote her thesis as soon as she said it. Under evidence he listed the map, the parish quotation and the interview as each appeared. Under reasoning he wrote the sentence that connected each piece to the claim, or a question mark when he could not find one. At the end he had a picture of the argument, not just a memory of the talk. That is *evaluative listening*: listening as a judge of the argument, not as a fan or a critic of the performer.

The three columns catch the three ways a talk can fail. A claim can be missing or so vague that nothing could count against it. Evidence can be missing, thin, or the wrong kind for the claim: one interview offered as proof of what a whole community thought. Reasoning, the link from evidence to claim, is the one listeners most often skip and speakers most often leave out; a speaker shows a striking image and moves on, and the audience supplies a link that was never argued. Write the question mark. Ask about it.

Separate the argument from the delivery. A confident speaker with a weak argument is more dangerous to your judgment than a nervous speaker with a strong one, because confidence feels like evidence and is not. Notice when you are being persuaded by the voice, the slides or the story rather than the reasoning, and check the columns. Notice, too, the opposite bias: a speaker who stumbles may have the best evidence in the room. Judge the page, not the performance. You will be asked to do exactly this for the rest of your life, by advertisements, by candidates, by people who want your money.

Listening well also means noticing what is not said. What alternative explanation did the speaker not mention? Which obvious source was absent? Where did the speaker's confidence rise just as the evidence thinned? Those are your questions, and a question built from careful listening is a gift to the speaker: it points at the place the work can improve. Dani's best question came from Jordan, who had listened for the one thing her talk left out. That is what a colleague does.

words.d: listening to judge an argument's claim, evidence and reasoning as they are presented
the stated link that explains why a piece of evidence supports the claim
the manner of a talk: voice, confidence, slides, pacing, as distinct from its argument

look.title: Marcus's Three Columns
rows: Reasoning links stated by the speaker
Question marks (links left to the audience)
look.cite: Marcus's listening notes on Dani's talk, written for this lesson
look.prompt: One piece of evidence was shown without a stated link to the claim. Why is that the most useful thing for Marcus to ask about afterward?

check.q: Which failure does the lesson say listeners most often miss?
choices: Missing reasoning: evidence shown without a stated link to the claim
check.why: Audiences supply the link themselves and never notice it was not argued.

check.q: Why is a confident speaker with a weak argument called dangerous to your judgment?
choices: Because confidence feels like evidence but is not
Because confident speakers talk too fast
check.why: Delivery can persuade in place of reasoning; the columns are the check.

check.q: A question built from careful listening is described as what?
choices: A gift, because it points at where the work can improve
check.why: The listener who notices what was left out helps the speaker most.

lessons.title: Feedback That Can Be Used
lessons.mainIdea: Useful feedback is specific, points at the work rather than the person, names one or two changes that matter most, and says what to keep.
reading: Three comments on Dani's talk. First: Great job, really interesting! Second: It was kind of confusing in the middle. Third: Your map slide worked; I could see the move without you explaining it. But when you showed the parish quotation, you went straight to the next point, and I did not know what you wanted me to take from it. One sentence after the quote would fix that. Only the third is *feedback*. The first is applause. The second is a feeling with no location. The third names a place, describes what happened for the listener, and suggests a change small enough to make.

Specific feedback has an address. Say where: the second slide, the transition into your last point, the answer to the first question. Say what you experienced there as a listener, not what the speaker did wrong: I lost the thread, I could not read the type, I was not sure whether that was your view or the source's. Reporting your own experience is both kinder and more accurate, because it is the one thing you know for certain. Then, if you can, suggest a fix, and make it the smallest fix that would work.

Choose. A speaker who receives twelve notes will fix none of them. Pick the one or two changes that would most improve the next version, and lead with those. Prioritizing is where the skill is: a wrong date on slide four matters less than a missing link between the evidence and the thesis, and the missing link matters less than a thesis nobody could state afterward. Say what to keep, too, and say why. Praise with a reason is information: the map slide worked because it showed the route without words. Praise without a reason is noise.

Receiving feedback is its own skill. Write it down without arguing; you can decide later what to use. Ask for the address if the note has none: where in the talk did it get confusing? Thank the person, especially for the hard note, because a hard note is a sign that someone took the work seriously. Then sort: which notes name the same problem, which ones would change the argument, and which are about taste. Fix the problems that several people named first. A single listener's confusion might be that listener; three listeners' confusion is the talk.

words.d: a specific report of what a listener experienced at a named point in the work, usually with a suggested change
choosing the one or two changes that matter most and leading with them
the exact place in a talk or paper a piece of feedback refers to

look.title: Rewrite the Note
look.text: A classmate's note on a talk reads: 'The beginning was kind of slow and I think you should have more evidence.' The speaker cannot use it. The talk opened with a two-minute history of the neighborhood before the question appeared, and its second point rested on a single newspaper article.
look.prompt: Rewrite the note so it has an address, reports the listener's experience, and suggests the smallest fix for each problem.

check.q: Why is 'It was kind of confusing in the middle' weak feedback?
choices: It reports a feeling with no address and no suggested change.
check.why: The speaker cannot find or fix a problem that has no location.

check.q: Why does the lesson prefer reporting your own experience over saying what the speaker did wrong?
choices: Because it is the one thing the listener knows for certain, and it is kinder
Because speakers never do anything wrong
check.why: I lost the thread here is accurate and usable; you were unclear is a guess about the speaker.

check.q: Three listeners were confused at the same point, and one listener was confused somewhere else. What does the lesson say?
choices: Fix the single listener's problem first
Fix the problem three people named first; one listener's confusion may be that listener
Ask the teacher which to fix
check.why: Repeated notes point at the talk; a single note may point at the listener.

lessons.title: Measuring Your Own Growth
lessons.mainIdea: Reflection compares specific earlier work with specific current work, names what changed and how, and sets the next thing to learn.
reading: Dani opened a paragraph she had written in ninth grade, an argument about school uniforms. It had a thesis, sort of: Uniforms are bad for many reasons. It had evidence, sort of: a friend's opinion and a website with no author. It had reasoning nowhere. She laughed, and then she did the useful thing: she wrote down exactly what her twelfth-grade paper did that the ninth-grade paragraph did not. A thesis someone could disagree with. Twelve sources she could defend. A paragraph where she weighed two accounts that conflicted. An answer to the strongest objection. That list is *reflection*, and it is worth more than the grade.

Reflection is not the same as feeling proud or feeling bad. It is a comparison with evidence, done to yourself. Put an early piece of work next to a late one and list the differences as specifically as you would in a research paper. Then ask how each change happened: which assignment, which piece of feedback, which habit. Dani traced her handling of conflicting sources to a synthesis grid a teacher made her fill out, which she had resented at the time. Knowing where a skill came from tells you how to get the next one.

Be honest about what has not changed. Dani still wrote introductions last and dreaded them, still overused the word significant, still ran long. A reflection that lists only strengths is a speech, not a reflection. The most useful sentence in one is often I still cannot, followed by the specific thing, followed by what I will try next. That sentence turns a weakness into a plan. It is also, not by accident, the same move as the honest answer to a question you cannot answer: here is what I do not know, and here is what it would take.

Keep the evidence. A folder with one piece of writing from each year, and a page of notes on what changed between them, is a *portfolio*, and it will be more useful to you than any transcript. It shows you, in your own words, that you can learn hard things, on the days when that is hard to believe. It also gives you something concrete to say when a college application or an interviewer asks how you have grown, a question nearly everyone answers with vague words and almost no one answers with a specific before and after.

words.d: an honest, specific comparison of earlier and later work that names what changed, how, and what comes next
a kept collection of your own work over time, with notes on what changed between pieces
a repeated practice, such as noting page numbers or drafting the body first, that a skill grows from

lessons.title: What to Carry Forward
lessons.mainIdea: The habits of this course, asking real questions, checking sources, crediting others, revising with readers and answering challenges honestly, are the same habits college and work reward.
reading: A first-year college assignment: read three articles that disagree, and write eight pages saying which is right and why. A first job: the manager asks you to find out why a process is failing, and to present what you found to people who will ask questions. A community meeting: someone claims a number, and you want to know where it came from. None of these says research paper. All of them are one. The habits you built in this unit are not school habits. They are the habits of anyone who has to find out what is true and say so in front of others.

Carry the question first. In college, the students who struggle most are often those who wait to be told what to think; the students who thrive have learned to ask an open, specific, arguable question and go looking. At work, the person who asks what would we need to know to decide this is the person who gets asked into the room where decisions are made. Carry the source habit: who wrote this, when, with what evidence, and who checked it. It will protect you from more than bad grades. Carry *attribution*: giving credit for ideas and words, which in a workplace is the difference between a colleague people trust and one they do not.

Carry the reader. Nothing you write will be as clear to others as it is to you, and the only cure is a reader before the deadline. Carry the calendar: long work is done in stages, and revision needs its own week. And carry the answer to the hard question: restate, concede what is true, hold what the evidence holds, mark the line. You will use that shape in seminars, in job interviews, in meetings, in arguments that matter to you. It is the sound of someone who has done the work and is not afraid of being asked about it.

Finally, carry the reading. You have spent years learning to read texts that resist: a sentence that will not open, a poem that means two things, a scholarly article written for someone else. That skill is not finished, and it never will be, but it is yours. Every hard document in your future, a lease, a contract, a study, a ballot measure, a policy at work, is a text that fights back, and you know how to read in passes, take it apart, look things up and come back. This unit ends here. The habit does not.

words.d: giving credit for ideas and words to the people they came from
a question that cannot be settled by one lookup or a yes or no, and so drives real inquiry
the separate dated steps of long work: question, sources, draft, reader, revision
